## Modeling the Distribution and Impact of Immunity to COVID-19

## in Populations

## Abstract

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has highlighted the need for scientifically-informed public health policies. Mathe-

matical modeling is an important tool to help evaluate possible interventions and better understand disease dynamics.

In this dissertation, I apply modeling approaches to evaluate vaccine allocation policies, and extend key takeaways

from this analysis to suggest how future vaccine allocation modeling should take equity into account. I also use

modeling to estimate the level of protective immunity conveyed by prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In Chapter 1, I first model efficiency and fairness in a vaccine prioritization strategy. At the time of initial

COVID-19 vaccination, when the number of vaccine doses available was limited, decisions had to be made on the

order in which different groups of people would be eligible for vaccination. After health-care workers and people

older than 75 years were made eligible, this case study compares next vaccinating either people 65-74 years old, or

other front-line workers. As the burden of COVID-19 infections and death is characterized by stark disparities in

age and race/ethnicity, I estimate both the number of lives saved and the number of years of life saved under each of

the policies, overall and in every race/ethnicity group, in the United States and every state.

Next, in Chapter 2, I expand on this work by conducting a methodological study of COVID-19 vaccine allocation

modeling papers, specifically looking for publications that considered equity. I provide examples of how modeling

can be useful to answer equity questions, and highlight some of the findings from the publications that did so. I also

highlight eight key considerations that are important to take into account when including equity in future vaccine

allocation models.

Finally, in Chapter 3, I estimate how infection-derived immunity protects against the Omicron variant among

unvaccinated individuals using a unique dataset from the Hutterite cohort study. I use a chain-binomial model

combining serological and virological surveillance data to model how prior infection affects susceptibility to infection

and infectiousness when infected. I also investigate the possible mechanism of protection and find that a leaky model

is the best fit, meaning that immune protection from prior infection is dependent on the force of infection.

## Introduction

The SARS-Cov-2 pandemic has highlighted the need for scientifically informed public health decision-making.

Mathematical modeling had been a key tool to help inform public policy, with great contributions in helping

understand and respond to central challenges of the pandemic. Mathematical modeling, generally, describes the

process of simplifying real-life systems into key elements that can be represented using mathematical concepts.

Infectious disease models can have a wide range in complexity, depending on the question of interest and the data

available3. Modeling is a key tool in infectious disease outbreaks: it can be used to provide new information from

data that is available, such as estimating parameters about novel pathogens from case data, as well as providing

insights into what may happen in the future, such as estimating potential impacts of disease control policies before

they are implemented.

In the example of the COVID-19 pandemic, modeling was used very early in the outbreak to estimate the basic

reproduction number, R0, which represents the number of secondary cases caused by one infected person in a

wholly susceptible population, which was an important indicator of the epidemic potential of this virus4,5,6. As soon

as estimates of important disease parameters were available, modeling was used to demonstrate the potential impact

of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) that could be or were implemented, such as lockdowns and reductions

1


<!-- Page 14 -->


in contacts7,8,9, face masking10, limitation in gathering sizes11,12, or school closures13,14. As these were put in place,

the effective reproduction number Rt, representing transmission over time, was also estimated15,8,16. Modeling was

also used to develop forecasts, which predicted cases, hospitalizations and deaths, allowing for resource planning17,9.

Longer-term scenario models were used to propose ways out of the pandemic, highlighting the need for vaccines to

build sufficient population immunity for contacts to go back to pre-2020 times18. And as vaccines became available,

mathematical models were used to identify the most efficient roll-out strategies and predict their impact as the

number of doses available increased, in the general population19 or specific settings such as nursing homes20.

The burden of COVID-19 diseases and deaths was strikingly unevenly distributed, both between regions and

countries of the world as well as within them. Some public health interventions aimed to respond to these unequal

health outcomes. In Chapter 1, I look at a case study that arose in discussions around the initial rollout of COVID-19

vaccines in the state of Massachusetts in 2021. Specifically, as the vaccine supply was initially very limited, groups

needed to be defined and given some order of access to vaccination. These groups were most frequently defined

by age or occupation. Particularly, the topic of debate was who should be eligible for vaccination after health-care

workers and people older than 75 years old, eligible, respectively, due to their benefit to society and their occupational

exposure, and exponentially growing mortality rate. Two options were suggested as the potential next group: people

aged 65-74, the next age band that experienced some of the increase in mortality with age, and (non-healthcare)

front-line due to the increased risk of infection they faced. One core discussion point is that the racial/ethnic

distribution is different between the two groups, which raised the question of equity in this allocation policy. In this

chapter, I show that allocating vaccines to the 65-74 year olds first saves more lives and years of life, both overall and

within every racial/ethnic group, in the United States as a whole and in almost every state.

This work highlighted broader questions around incorporating equity into models of COVID-19 vaccine

allocation. One of our conclusions was that who received most vaccines does not necessarily align with whose lives

are being saved. Another key result was that age and race/ethnicity are both positively associated with critical health

outcomes, including COVID-19 mortality at the time of vaccine roll-out, and negatively correlated with one another

in the United States and other countries. This leads to opposite vaccine prioritization being made depending on

which variable is used to define eligibility groups. We wondered if the insights from our case study were generalizable,

if other publications had run into similar patterns, and overall how modelers approached questions related to equity

in vaccine allocation. In Chapter 2, I conduct a review of the modeling literature for initial COVID-19 vaccines

allocation, specifically looking for publications that took equity into account. I find few publications that did, but

highlight advice for future models that may aim to answer these types of questions.

<!-- Page 15 -->


Finally, inChapter3, I usemodeling tomeasurethe impacts ofCOVID-19infection-derivedimmunity. Iestimate

how an immune response due to an infection with SARS-CoV-2 with one of the strains circulating before Omicron,

protects from Omicron infection in early 2022. Because of widespread vaccination and varying vaccination histories,

answering this question is complicated. I am able to measure this using a unique dataset, the Hutterites cohort

study. Hutterites are a religious group who live in small communities in rural Canada and choose not to get mRNA

vaccines and were mostly unvaccinated against SARS-CoV-2, thus acting as a sort of ‘natural experiment’ in which

we can assume that any antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 come from a previous infection. They live in very tight-knit

and relatively small colonies of about 100 people, which likely allows for daily aerosol contacts between colony

members. The study followed members of Hutterite colonies in Canada, collecting both longitudinal serology data

providing information on antibody levels, and weekly virological tests that detect infections. Using a chain-binomial

model, I look at how much this immunity affects the risk of infection (i.e. how much it reduces susceptibility)

and how much it changes the risk of onward transmission (i.e. how much it reduces infectiousness). I then use a

dose-response model to estimate how the quantity of antibodies lowers the probability of infection. These results

can also help us better understand the dynamics of transmission for people who have acquired immunity from

an infection when a new variant emerges, and to compare that protection to that provided by vaccination. These

methods of combining serological and virological surveillance may also help us to obtain these answers more quickly

for the next pandemic.

## 1

## Fairness and efficiency considerations in

## COVID-19 vaccine allocation strategies:

## a case study comparing front-line

## workers and 65–74 year olds

## in the United States

### 1.1 Abstract

The COVID-19 epidemic in the United States has been characterized by two stark disparities. COVID-19

burden has been unequally distributed among racial and ethnic groups and at the same time the mortality rates have

been sharply higher among older age groups. These disparities have led some to suggest that inequalities could be

reduced by vaccinating front-line workers before vaccinating older individuals, as older individuals in the US are

4


<!-- Page 17 -->


disproportionately Non-Hispanic White. We compare the performance of two distribution policies, one allocating

vaccines to front-line workers and another to older individuals aged 65-74-year-old. We estimate both the number of

lives saved and the number of years of life saved under each of the policies, overall and in every race/ethnicity groups,

in the United States and every state. We show that prioritizing COVID-19 vaccines for 65-74-year-olds saves both

more lives and more years of life than allocating vaccines front-line workers in each racial/ethnic group, in the United

States as a whole and in nearly every state. When evaluating fairness of vaccine allocation policies, the overall benefit

to impact of each population subgroup should be considered, not only the proportion of doses that is distributed to

each subgroup. Further work can identify prioritization schemes that perform better on multiple equity metrics.

### 1.2 Introduction

Two stark disparities define the mortality impact of the COVID-19 epidemic in the United States. The risk of

death given infection (infection fatality rate) rises sharply with age. By one estimate, this increase is exponential,

about 10-fold for each 19-year increase in age21. Another estimate fits a linear increase and finds a 1.18 percentage-

point absolute increase in infection fatality rate per decade of age22. At the same time, Black, Hispanic, and Native

American persons in the US have experienced confirmed infections, hospitalizations, and deaths at dramatically

higher rates than White or Asian persons23, reflecting a pattern of racial/ethnic and socioeconomic disparity that is

observed also in other populations24,25,26,27. As of March 2021, White and Asian populations in the US have similar

age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates (respectively 121/100,000 and 117/100,000). Compared to White populations,

the age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rate is 1.7-fold higher among Black populations (241/100,000), 1.9-fold higher

among Indigenous populations (263/100,000), 2.0-fold higher among Hispanic populations (287/100,000) and

2.2-fold higher among Pacific Islander populations (312 / 100,000)28. An additional relevant fact that connects these

two disparities is that White and Asian populations are older on average than Black, Hispanic, and other racial/ethnic

groups in the United States.

The two risk factors of age and race, as well as their interaction, have received attention in discussions on vaccine

prioritization. While prioritization of older adults and individuals with comorbid conditions predisposing them to

higher infection-fatality rates is under most scenarios expected to save more lives in the aggregate than non-prioritized

strategies29,30? ,18, such a strategy in the US involves providing more vaccine doses, earlier, to White individuals

and fewer to Black, Hispanic, Asian and Native American people, due to the differences in age distribution. An

alternative strategy, that of prioritizing essential or front-line workers, has been discussed as a way to provide more

5


<!-- Page 18 -->


vaccine doses to those racial/ethnic groups that are hardest hit by COVID-19, because essential workers are more

ethnically and racially diverse than older individuals in the US.

Here we quantify the potential impacts overall and by race/ethnicity, comparing two groups that have been

widely discussed for prioritization below long-term care residents and health care workers and those 75 and older,

but above other members of the population: i) individuals 65–74 not in long-term care or nursing homes, and ii)

front-line (non health care) workers. For the United States and each state individually, we quantify the extent to

which these two policies would provide vaccines to members of different racial and ethnic groups, and we ask the

further question of how the two policies compare in terms of expected lives and years of life saved overall and for

each racial/ethnic group.

Such estimates require certain modeling assumptions. We outline those in detail in Methods, but we emphasize

here the most important. First, we consider only the direct effects of vaccination in preventing death from COVID-

19 in vaccinated persons. Indirect effects on transmission are not considered in this study, to simplify and make

transparent the analysis and because vaccines’ effects on transmission were not clear at the time of vaccine allocation

decisions. Second, we make the assumption that from the moment the prioritization decision is made, future

COVID-19 deaths in strata defined by age group, race/ethnicity and state, and occupation (essential worker or not)

are proportional to those estimated for the period prior to January 30, 2021. This assumption links future disparities

in death rates related to all these factors to past ones. Third, we assume that vaccine uptake and effectiveness is even

across race/ethnic groups within an age group and state under each policy; we discuss the impact of this assumption

later. The second and third assumptions together enable a comparison of the projected number of lives saved in

each race/ethnicity, by state, by allocating a fixed number of vaccine doses under each of the two policies.

### 1.3 Methods

1.3.1 Notation

We repeat our analyses across multiple age categories, race/ethnicity groups and US states. We consider various

geographical entities k: either the entirety of the United States, or any one of 50 states or the District of Columbia.

The age groups considered are either 65-74 year old for policy S, or 16-64 (further detailed into 16-24, 25-34, 35-44,

45-54, 55-64) for front-line workers for policy F. We conducted our analyses for seven race/ethnicity categories (Non-

Hispanic Whites, Hispanics, Non-Hispanic Blacks or African American, Non-Hispanic Asians, Non-Hispanic Two

or more races, Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native, Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or other Pacific

1.3.2 Data sources and estimation

1.3.2.1 Estimating the number of COVID-19 deaths outside of nursing homes and long term

care facilities by state, race/ethnicity and age categories

We obtained the number of COVID-19 deaths by state, age, race and Hispanic origin group reported to the

National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) between January 1st 2020 and January 30th 202132. We also extracted

the proportion of COVID-19 deaths that took place outside of nursing homes and long term care facilities between

January 4th 2020 and January 30th 2021, by state and age categories from the NCHS33. Deaths counts ranging

between 1 and 9, which were not reported due to the NCHS confidentiality standards, were approximated by the

median value 5.

As nursing home and long-term care facilities residents and employees have access to vaccination before 65-74

and front-line workers, we do not consider deaths that took place in those settings as part of our analysis. Assuming

that this proportion of COVID-19 deaths in nursing homes and long term care facilities is constant across races and

ethnicity for a given state and age category, we compute the proportion of COVID-19 deaths that took place outside

### 1.5 Discussion

The burden of COVID-19 infections and deaths has been unequally distributed among racial and ethnic groups

in the US, while deaths have been sharply higher among older age groups. The ethical imperatives of saving the most

lives and minimizing inequalities have led to debate about age- and occupation-based criteria for prioritizing access

to vaccines when they are scarce38,39,40. Because the hardest-hit racial and ethnic groups in the US also have younger

age distributions, prioritization schemes that favor older ages intrinsically provide fewer vaccines to members of

these disadvantaged groups, as we quantify in Table S1.3. This consideration has led some to suggest that fairness

goals could be better achieved by prioritizing vaccines for front-line workers, a category that has greater exposure to

infection, has high pandemic-related excess mortality41, and that includes members of highly-affected racial and

ethnic groups.

One might expect that a policy such as prioritizing front-line workers, which provides more vaccine doses to

Black, Hispanic, and Asian persons than prioritizing 65–74 year olds, would also save more lives in these non-White

groups. On the other hand, some have argued that this is unlikely because for each race/ethnicity, risk of death in-

creases dramatically with age, and providing more doses to relatively young members of the hardest-hit groups ahead

of (a smaller number of) older members of these groups misses the opportunity to prevent deaths in these groups.

Consistent with this latter argument, we have shown that in the United States as a whole and in nearly every state, a

front-line worker prioritization saves fewer lives in each racial/ethnic group than prioritization of 65-74-year-olds, at

least when considering the direct effects of vaccination in protecting the vaccinated person. Specifically, prioritizing

65–74 year olds is projected to save 3.5 times as many Hispanic lives, 5.1 times as many non-Hispanic Black, 5.0 times

as many non-Hispanic Asian lives, 3.0 times as many Non-Hispanic American Indian and Alaska Native lives, 1.5

times as many Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, 2.7 times as many non-Hispanic multiracial

lives, and 9.3 times more non-Hispanic White lives than prioritizing front-line workers. Simply put, this is because

the dramatically higher COVID-19 mortality rates in older persons (ranging from 2.6 to 7.5 fold by our estimates for

the different race/ethnicity groups) outweigh the more modest differences in representation of these groups among

different races (ranging from 1.1-fold for Asians to 2.8-fold for individuals with two or more races). This is likely

driven by the over-representation of younger adults among the front-line workers when compared to the general

population (Supplementary Figure S1.2). In short, Blacks, Hispanics, Asians, American Indians and Alaska Natives,

Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islanders and individuals with more than one race get somewhat more vaccines

19


<!-- Page 32 -->


under a front-line worker priority, but those vaccines go to individuals at much lower risk of dying.

This finding demonstrates by example that it is possible to choose a vaccine distribution strategy that provides a

more equal vaccine distribution by race/ethnicity, yet prevents fewer deaths in every racial/ethnic group. Under our

assumptions, if one considers vaccines as means to the ends of saving lives, the greater number of lives saved under

the age-based policy, including in the hardest-hit groups, should lead one to favor the age-based policy over the

front-line-worker policy regardless of how one weighs overall societal benefit and benefit to the hardest-hit groups,

because the age-based policy maximizes both.

Our model relies on multiple simplifying modeling assumptions. We assume that (i) the vaccine efficacy and

uptake is constant across age, race and location, (ii) the proportion of deaths that took place in nursing homes and

long-term care facilities is constant across races for a given age and state (an assumption made because nursing home

status of deaths is given by age and state, but not race), (iii) 10% of deaths recorded for the 15–24 year old category

took place among 15 year olds, (iv) that we can account for the increased risk of infection and deaths among front-line

workers by multiplying the mortality rate by an increased risk R constant across age, race and state, and that (v)

analyses by Mutambudzi et al.31 appropriately estimate this R.

We have shown in sensitivity analyses that the increase in infection risk for front-line workers would need to

be larger than 3 for a policy vaccinating front-line workers over 65–74 year olds to become preferable for some

race/ethnicity groups (Supplementary Tables S1.5 and S1.7). Such large values would be more likely to happen during

lock-down periods, when public-facing workers have much larger contact rates than the rest of the population. If

vaccines are being rolled-out during such periods, then a policy allocating doses to front-line workers first may be

preferable.

Our analysis is subject to other limitations. First, we focus our analysis on two outcomes: deaths and years

of life lost. We did not assess the impact of the two vaccination policies on other outcomes such as number of

infections, morbidity such as long COVID42, hospitalization or other economic consequences. As it has been show

that vaccination strategies targeting younger adults can lead to lower number of infections but higher number of

deaths29, it is possible that vaccinating front-line workers would lead to fewer infections. Second, we assume that the

number of deaths occurring after vaccine allocation and roll-out is proportional to the death count up to January 30,

20


<!-- Page 33 -->


2021 (more exactly is it assumed to be equal to 20% of the cumulative deaths up to that date in each age, race and state

combination). We thus assume that the inequalities in infection and mortality rates stay constant over the duration

of the pandemic. Third, we only consider the direct effect of vaccination on the vaccinated, and not the indirect

effect of vaccination protecting the rest of the population by limiting onward transmission. When this work began,

it was unclear how to what extent COVID-19 vaccines reduce transmission43. While evidence is now accumulating

for substantial vaccine effects on infection and onward spread44, these results reflect the knowledge available at the

time prioritization decisions were being made. Moreover, as the B.1.617.2 (Delta) and B.1.1.529 (Omicron) variants

have become dominant worldwide, doubts on vaccine efficacy against it are being raised45. If the protection against

transmission of Delta, Omicron, and future variants is indeed found to be limited, vaccine allocation strategies

should focus on direct protection from infection. The magnitude of the relative benefit of the 65–74 strategy over

the front-line strategy via direct protection studied here suggests that the greater indirect effects of vaccinating

front-line workers would have to be large to make it superior in preventing deaths in any racial/ethnic group, or

overall. Front-line workers and members of racial/ethnic minorities46 may be more likely to live in multi-generation

households and contribute to more onward transmission than 65–74 year old individuals. Mulberry et al.47 studied

the indirect effect of vaccination (without considering race/ ethnicity) using an age-stratified SEIR model including

compartment for essential workers. Under strong assumptions that drastic social distancing measured are in place

(no workplace contacts for non-essential workers and all contacts reduced), that the impact of vaccination of trans-

mission is strong, and that Rt is not kept at very low levels, they showed that vaccinating essential workers and/or all

adults 20–79 after individuals over 80 leads to lower number of infections, hospitalization and deaths than a solely

age-based strategy. Further work is needed to understand these tradeoffs and the extent to which accounting for

indirect protection might reverse our findings under the rapidly changing conditions of COVID-19.

Notwithstanding these limitations, we have shown that from the perspective of infections directly prevented, a

front-line-worker COVID-19 vaccine prioritization strategy does not save as many lives and years of life as prioritiza-

tion of 65–74 year olds, overall or in each racial/ethnic group, and that this effect is qualitatively consistent across US

states.

Although these two strategies received the most attention from committees considering prioritization schemes,

there may be other strategies that might outperform either one, as some work has already suggested. For example,

once health-care workers and individuals aged 65+ are vaccinated, prioritizing adults at increased risk of severe

21


<!-- Page 34 -->


COVID-19 would increase access to vaccines for Non-Hispanic Blacks, while Hispanics would receive most doses

under a strategy targeting essential workers and Non-Hispanic Whites and Asians under a solely age-based strategy48.

For the goal of saving the most lives with a prevention intervention such as vaccination, it is optimal to prioritize

individuals in order of their estimated mortality risk from the disease, which is the product of the mortality risk

if infected (the infection-fatality risk) and their probability of becoming infected (a function of exposure). It is

evident in the United States and elsewhere, at least from the pandemic history to date, that both older age and

non-White race or Hispanic ethnicity are associated with higher risks49. Mortality risk at a given age varies with

racial/ethnic classification, as for instance, in the US in 2020 Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaskan Native aged

35–44 and Hispanic individuals aged 45–54 had higher mortality rates than Non-Hispanic White individuals aged

55–64 (Supplementary Figure S1.3). It follows that a policy that allocated vaccine priority according to this criterion

would at each age prioritize Black and Hispanic individuals over White ones, and would assign equal priority, all

other factors being equal, to a younger Hispanic or Black individual as to an older White one50. A version of this

approach–lower age cutoffs for Black persons to receive priority–has been proposed51 and would both enhance

equity and, if done appropriately, also enhance the number of lives saved overall and for Black Americans compared

to an age-only prioritization. Likewise, geographic targeting to areas of high risk would increase racial equity while

improving access to vaccination for those at greater risk of death from COVID-1950. Overall, questions related to

the fairness of vaccine prioritization are most important when vaccine distribution is slow. If the roll-out is rapid,

the difference in the benefit from different strategies diminishes, as all individuals get access to vaccines at similar

times regardless of their age, race/ethnicity and occupation.

## Equity considerations in COVID-19

## vaccine allocation modeling:

## a methodological study

### 2.6 Abstract

We conducted a methodological study of COVID-19 vaccine allocation modeling papers, specifically looking

for publications that considered equity. We found that most models did not take equity into account, with the vast

majority of publications presenting aggregated results and no results by any subgroup (e.g. age, race, geography, etc.).

We then provide examples of how modeling can be useful to answer equity questions, and highlight some of the

findings from the publications that did. Finally, we describe eight considerations that seem important to consider

when including equity in future vaccine allocation models.

23


<!-- Page 36 -->


### 2.7 Introduction

As COVID-19 vaccines became available in 2021, countries and regions around the globe had to define criteria

for prioritizing access to vaccines. For example, WHO’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization

(SAGE) released a roadmap in October 2020 for prioritizing uses of COVID-19 vaccines in the context of limited

supply. In situations of community transmission, they recommended vaccines be first given to healthcare workers

and older individuals, followed by groups (defined by health states or sociodemographic status) at significantly

higher risk of severe disease and deaths52. Similarly, in the United States, the Advisory Committee on Immunization

Practices recommended vaccines be allocated first to health-care personnel and residents of long-term care facilities,

followed by older individuals, people with high-risk medical conditions and essential workers not already included53.

Some have argued that vaccine allocation should provide equitable protection of individuals and should aim to

reduce (or at least not further increase) inequities in health burden. For example, WHO’s SAGE developed a values

framework for the allocation and prioritization of COVID-19 vaccines, defining six core principles for equitable

protection. In addition to human well-being, equal respect, reciprocity and legitimacy, two of the principles were

global equity (i.e. vaccine access to all countries, particularly low- and middle-income countries) and national equity

(i.e. preferential allocation for vulnerable groups and groups experiencing higher burden)54. Similarly, the United

States National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, in its 2020 Framework for equitable allocation

of COVID-19 vaccine, defined three ethical principles: maximum benefit, equal concern and mitigation of health

inequities, defined as the obligation to explicitly address the higher burden of COVID-19 experienced by some

populations40.

Modeling has provided useful contributions to identify the best performing allocation strategies for COVID-

19 vaccines and has helped inform policy making in the face of uncertainty about the vaccines and pathogens

characteristics. Many publications have modelled the performance of different allocation strategies, often comparing

transmission-minimizing approaches targeting younger adults with mortality-minimizing approaches targeting

older age groups when vaccine stock is limited29,18,30? .

Despite huge inequities in disease burden distribution and large modeling literature on allocation optimization,

however, few publications modelled equity considerations. Here, we present a methodological study conducted to

identify publications that looked at equity and COVID-19 vaccine allocation modeling. We highlight some of their

main findings and summarize advice to modellers wanting to include equity in future models.

### 2.8 Methods

We conducted a literature review and expert-opinion elicitation in search of papers that looked at COVID-19

vaccine allocation, presenting outcomes stratified by any characteristic (age, race, ethnicity, occupation, geography,

etc.). Our goal was to be as broad as possible and identify publications that presented results by any subgroup, even

if the idea of equity was not the focus of the publication.

We performed a literature review using PubMed, including studies published between 2019 and May 2024. We

included all peer-reviewed publications and pre-prints that were relevant to our search terms for:

• COVID-19: COVID-19 Vaccines[MeSH] OR SARS-CoV*[ti] OR COVID*[ti] OR coronavir*[ti] OR

NCOV[ti]

• Vaccine: vaccine*[ti] OR vaccination[ti]

• Modeling: ”Computer Simulation“[Mesh] OR ”Epidemiological Models”[Mesh] OR ”Models, Statisti-

cal”[Mesh] OR model*[ti] OR scenario[ti] OR strategies[ti] OR strategy[ti] OR prioritization[ti]

• Disparityorsubpopulation: Demography[Majr]OR”PopulationGroups,US”[Mesh]OR”AgeFactors”[Mesh]

OR ”Race Factors”[Mesh] OR Aged[Mesh] OR demographic*[ti] OR equit*[tiab] OR inequit*[tiab] OR

OR aged[ti] OR elder*[ti] OR ”risk factor*”[ti] OR “Health Equity”[Mesh]

From this search, we identified 253 papers to be reviewed, as listed in Supplementary able S2.1. After review, six

of them corresponded to our criterion for inclusion.

To look for additional relevant studies, we carried out a manual search of all studies cited or citing the papers we

had already identified and found an additional six publications.

Finally, having found only a limited number of research papers that met our criteria in the literature review, we

conducted an expert-opinion elicitation to identify research papers that we may have missed. We contacted four

experts in public health and the study of disparities, asking if they knew of publications matching our criteria. All

provided publications we had identified already. The experts were (in alphabetical order) Dr. Mary Bassett (MD,

MPH), Harvard University, Dr. Mathew Kiang (MPH, ScD), Stanford University, Dr. Andrew C. Stokes (MA,

PhD), Boston University and Dr. Elizabeth Wrigley-Field (MA, PhD), University of Minnesota.

Our methodological study has limitations. Firstly, although we searched for the most publications possible by

doing both a literature review and expert-opinion elicitation, there may be publications that we missed. It can be

25


<!-- Page 38 -->


especially difficult to identify publications as not all explicitly mention equity, and some use diverse vocabulary

to describe similar analyses. We are also more likely to have missed publications that looked at inequity across

variables other than race/ethnicity or age, such as pre-existing conditions, place of residence, sex, religion, education

or SES, for example55. The search terms we used and the experts we reached out to likely biased our results towards

publications from the United States. They may also have biased our results towards publications in the infectious

disease modeling field, leading us to miss some literature in other fields such as decision science. Secondly, we focused

our literature search on prioritization of COVID-19 initial vaccination. We did not include publications regarding

allocation of boosters as these took place under fewer vaccine quantity constraints.

### 2.9 Methodological study findings

Of the numerous publications that modelled COVID-19 vaccine allocation, most did not explicitly consider

equity. Despite an extended search directed at literature considering equity between population subgroups and

manual review of 253 publications, only six (2.4%)56,57,58,59,60,2 were COVID-19 vaccine allocation modeling studies

presenting results by some sub-group. From manual search among studies cited or citing those studies, we identified

an additional six publications61,62,63,50,64,65. Expert-opinion elicitation of four experts did not provide any additional

publications. Of these, 11 explicitly consider equity in their model and one57 strives to identify the optimal allocation

without explicitly mentioning equity. Characteristics and key findings from these 12 publications can be found in

*Table 2.1.*

Contrary to the hypothesis of an equity/efficiency trade-off, there often is no such trade-off found, or it is

weaker than one might expect. Indeed, it can be possible to minimize total deaths or infections while simultaneously

reducing disparities between groups in the risks of these outcomes. Six publications have found that among the

vaccine allocation each considered, the most efficient policy overall is also the one most beneficial to one or multiple

structurally disadvantaged groups58,60,1,61,63,50. Notably, Chen et al. show that prioritizing the most disadvantaged

basedonanycriteria(age, race/ethnicity, occupationorincome)increasesbothequity(whichtheydefineasmitigation

of mortality disparities in disadvantaged demographic group) and social utility (which they define as minimizing

mortality in the entire population)61. Rumpler et al. show that a vaccine allocation policy targeting older individuals

saves most lives overall and among every racial/ethnic group, despite leading to fewer vaccines allocated to non-White

people than an allocation policy targeting non-healthcare frontline workers1. Wrigley-Field et al. show that targeting

racial/ethnic groups (or geography) makes vaccines available to people with higher mortality rates, and also increases

the proportion of non-White people eligible50. Kadelka et al. show that taking race/ethnicity into account when

26


<!-- Page 39 -->


prioritizing vaccines may reduce the total number of deaths, especially when also assuming that proportionately

more people of colour occupy high-contact jobs58. Rosenstrom et al. show that a strategy to increase vaccination

uptake in non-White individuals reduces deaths overall without significantly increasing the infection rate60. Stafford

et al. find that to minimize disease burden (death), the age cutoff for vaccine eligibility should be younger for people

of colour than for White people, suggesting that universal age thresholds are not the most efficient63. While there are

numerous instances of policies that improve equity and efficiency simultaneously compared to alternatives, we note

that definitions of equity can vary and that maximizing one aspect may not maximize all. We discuss this further

below.

Researchers face trade-offs in formulating research questions and performing the analyses to answer these

questions. A first trade-off is between considering allocation policies that are complex and may be optimal versus

considering simpler policies that may be more realistic. Nine publications looked at allocation rules that consider

only one or two characteristics (e.g. race, age, occupation, etc.)56,59,60,1,62,63,50,64,65. Three other studies looked for the

one optimal policy over multiple stratifying variables. The latter usually performs better but may be more difficult

to implement due to a high number of variables used to define allocation priority, and may not be generalizable

to other populations with different joint distributions of predictors and outcomes57,58,61. Kadelka et al. show that

increasing the number of levels within each parameter can also lead to better performance58.

A second trade-off may exist between acceptability (political, social or legal) and equity focused on certain dimensions,

such as race/ethnicity or age66,51,39,67. Indeed, while four publications consider vaccine allocation by race/ethnicity

categories directly58,60,61,63, others like Wrigley-Field et al. propose using geography-based vaccine allocation at the

census-tract level as an alternative to race/ethnicity strategies50. Three other papers57,64,65 consider geographical

units at various levels (county, states, country, etc.) as targets for vaccination.

Overall, comparing results from these 12 publications is made difficult by the fact that they use different

terms and vocabulary, sometimes without clear definitions, as we discuss further below. This may in part be due to the

fact that they come from different literatures: for example, the two publications from decision science journals64,65

contrast with some of the infectious disease modeling ones58,60,61,63.

### 2.10 Discussion

This methodological study provides insights for future vaccine allocation models that consider equity. These

are not specific to COVID-19 and could be applied to models for other epidemics, including but not limited to

pandemic influenza:

— Most modeling studies could show some results by subgroup, even if the focus of the paper is

not equity considerations. Indeed, most publications could easily show how the outcomes are distributed by

subgroups, instead of only showing total outcome in the population. This is especially true for COVID-19 models

that often have to include age categories due to the exponential increase in mortality rate with age: results by age

groups are already being generated and could easily be presented. As an example of how this can be done and how it

enhances the understanding of results, Chapman et al. show the distribution of vaccinations, as well as infections,

death and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) averted in each age group when the oldest age group (≥60 year

olds) is targeted for vaccination (after initial allocation to healthcare workers and long-term care facility residents)57.

— When modeling equity considerations in vaccine allocation, one should carefully choose the outcome

to be maximized. While most publications we found aimed at limiting some form of health burden (such as cases,

deaths, DALYs or years of life lost), some described the performance of each strategy in terms of doses allocated to

disadvantaged groups. Kipnis et al., for example, present total health outcome reduction of six different allocation

strategies, but present the results by subgroup (race/ethnicity and high neighbourhood deprivation index) in terms

of doses allocated59. An example of an alternative can be found in Hoover et al., where the impact of California’s

COVID-19 vaccine equity policy is shown on both vaccine administered and COVID-19 cases62. In some situations,

maximizing the number of vaccine doses given to a group does not necessarily maximize the number of lives saved

overall or in that group1. This underscores the importance of reporting both allocations and outcomes by group

and giving a rationale for what is being maximized. Additionally, the choice of health outcomes and how they

were collected (patient reporting, test result or physician assessment) can have consequences for equity68,69. This is

illustrated by Stafford et al., who show that minimizing different measures (here deaths or years of life lost) leads to

different disparities63.

— While it is preferable to stratify by multiple variables (as it is done by many publications57,59,60,63,50), some

models have considered vaccine allocation by only one variable56,1,61. When modeling vaccine allocation by one

variable only, the choice of the variable can have unexpected consequences for equity. This is, for example,

the case when comparing allocations by age groups and by race/ethnicity in the US. Indeed, as illustrated in one

34


<!-- Page 47 -->


case study1, those two variables are both associated with COVID-19 health outcomes (in the United States, older

individuals, as well as Hispanic, Black, Native and Pacific Islander have higher COVID-19 death rates), and negatively

associated with one another (in the United States, older individuals are disproportionately non-Hispanic White)

and therefore under a specific set of assumptions, basing an allocation on race/ethnicity could lead to more deaths

in each race/ethnicity stratum than basing it on age, even though race/ethnicity is very strongly associated with

mortality.

— The studies identified show diverse examples of how models can address equity considerations.

‘Equity’andrelatedconceptsmeandifferentthingstodifferentresearchers. Forexample,somepublicationsemphasize

equity as it relates specifically to the outcomes in the model and attempt to minimize inequality measures (which

may be relative60 or absolute56,59). Others note categories of preexisting disadvantage due to racism or geography,

for example, and focus on how to improve outcomes for already-disadvantaged groups58,61,63. A way to improve the

comparability of model predictions would be to present absolute outcomes (e.g. number of lives saved or lost) and

allocations (for example number of vaccines administered) by subgroup and overall, allowing a reader to calculate

disparity measures of particular interest, which may be relative or absolute, and may focus on particular subgroups

of the population. For example, Wrigley-Field et al. show on the same plots both the death rate in the population, as

well as the proportion of non-White people eligible for vaccination50.

— Data limitations can have implications for the questions being modeled. For example, the nine

publications that used data sources from the United States all included race/ethnicity in their model. As detailed

in table 2.1, the way race/ethnicity was coded varied widely between publications, with the number of race/ethnic

categories ranging from 258,63, 456,57,59,60,50, 61 up to 761. Additionally, some used single-race categories56,57,59,60,50,

while others included groups for individuals reporting two or more races1,61. While this is likely a result of data

limitations, modellers should be conscious that classification of race and ethnicity is a choice with implications for

equity and the inclusion of minorities70? ,71,72. Data limitations may impact outcome choice too, which, as described

above, can lead to different results.

— Care should be taken in model inputs that reflect already existing inequalities, such as life ex-

pectancy measures. The impact of a policy on life expectancy can be calculated using either population averages or

stratum-specific estimates of years of life left. For example, although life expectancy often varies by races/ethnicities73,

an average population-wide life expectancy is often used for all individuals of a given age in order to avoid down-

grading the value of saving the life of a person of a structurally disadvantaged racial/ethnic group1. Using the

average life expectancy may thus improve the number of vaccines allocated to people of structurally disadvantaged

35


<!-- Page 48 -->


race/ethnicities, but in doing so may reduce the total years of life saved. When considering age groups, however, it is

common to use age-specific life expectancy estimates, even if doing so downgrades the number of vaccines allocated

to older individuals to increase the total years of life saved. These opposite choices may or may not be justified, but

the fact that it is common to make opposite choices on these two demographic dimensions emphasizes that the

choice of which measure to use is an ethical one about how to balance efficiency and equity, rather than a purely

scientific one.

—MostCOVID-19vaccineallocationstudieswereconductedandpublishedinthefaceofsignificantuncertainty

about pathogen characteristics and transmission dynamics. Most of the papers we found57,58,59,63,50? dealt with

this by showing the robustness of their results across sensitivity analyses, thus strengthening the argument for the

allocation policies they identified as best. For example, Kadelka et al. replicated all their results varying scenarios

defined by three parameters of interest (ethnic homophily, relative contact level in high-contact versus low-contact

jobs, and relative proportion of people of colour compared to White people in high-contact jobs)58. In addition to

show robustness of results over parameters that may be uncertain or may change over time, it is important

to consider robustness over parameter distributions that may vary in different settings, such as age or

race/ethnicity. For example, Wrigley-Field et al. compare results in two US states (California and Minnesota) that

have different demographics50.

— Some of the papers considered only the direct protection from vaccination on those receiving it, not the

indirect effect on the rest of their communities57,1,50. Doing so can be tempting, as indirect effects may not happen

and can be more difficult to model with certainty, especially at the time allocation decisions are being made. Direct

protection of vaccination is always a useful metric and may be more robust to assumptions on vaccine protection

against infection or emergence of new variants. However, as highlighted by Jia et al., direct effects may not necessarily

represent a lower bound of overall effects of vaccination, for example, when vaccine wanes or when transmission or

fatality parameters increase over time, and should not be interpreted as such74.

## protection against COVID-19

## in Hutterite communities

### 3.11 Abstract

The protection against SARS-CoV-2 from a previous infection is difficult to estimate due to high rates of

vaccination and imperfect surveillance. Here, we estimate how infection-derived immunity protects against the

Omicron variant among unvaccinated individuals using a unique dataset from the Hutterite cohort study. Hutterites

are an Anabaptist religious group living in isolated communities of about a hundred people. We use a chain-binomial

model combining serological and virological surveillance data to estimate how infection-derived immunity protects

against Omicron infection. We find that antibody titers from prior infection are associated with a decrease in risk of

re-infection of up to 66% for the highest titer values. We also investigate the possible mechanism of protection and

find that a leaky model is the best fit, meaning that immune protection from prior infection is dependent on the

37


<!-- Page 50 -->


force of infection. We also investigate how pre-existing immunity impacts the infectiousness when reinfected and

find no statistical evidence of protection. These results help better understand how infection-derived immunity

works for COVID-19, particularly in the context of new variant emergence. The model can be used for future

epidemics and the parameters can inform model parametrization.

### 3.12 Introduction

The Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant emerged in November 2021 and rapidly spread throughout the world,

becoming dominant in during spring 202275. This variant is characterized by numerous mutations that make it

less virulent and more transmissible compared to previously circulating variants76,77,78,79. By this time a significant

portion of the world population had some immune protection against SARS-CoV-2 from infection with previous

variants, vaccination, oramixofboth. Evaluatingtheprotectionconferredbyinfection-derivedimmunityspecifically

is complex due to antecedent infections that are often asymptomatic or unrecorded, and complex hybrid immunity

with a wide range of vaccine coverage and platforms used.

In this study we estimate how immune response from prior infection protects against the Omicron variant in a

unique unvaccinated population residing in Hutterite colonies in Canada. Previous publications have evaluated

the protection conferred by pre- Omicron infection-derived immunity against infection with the Omicron variant

among unvaccinated people or adjusting for vaccination status, and found 40% reduction in susceptibility80,81,82.

Relatively few studies have investigated how naturally-acquired antibody titers can serve as correlate of protection

from re-infection with Omicron83,84,85,86. We develop a method for estimating a dose-response relationship between

antibody titers and protection from reinfection using a chain-binomial model. This method also allows us to look at

the mechanism of protection from prior infection. In a leaky protection, the risk of infection scales with the density

or number of infectious contacts (making proportional protection from immunity less effective when there are

multiple opportunities to become infected), but does not for an all-or-nothing protection, where the people with

immunity are considered to be fully protected87,88. Previous consideration of this question has been limited to one

other study, which found evidence of a leaky protection89. Lastly, we also contribute to the limited literature90,91,89

on the impact of immunity from a prior infection on the infectiousness when re-infected.

We do this in the Hutterite Cohort Study, which poses a unique opportunity to study SARS-CoV-2 transmission

in unvaccinated populations. Hutterites are Anabaptists living in community structures of about 100 people called

colonies, who have been enrolled in frequent serology and virological surveillance for much of the COVID-19

pandemic. While they do not oppose all vaccination, they decided not to use mRNA vaccine technology and the vast

38


<!-- Page 51 -->


majority of the colony members are unvaccinated. Weekly virological testing allows for high quality characterization

of infections independently of symptoms, and close tight-knit structure of colonies makes the random mixing

assumption more tenable. Frequent serology testing, including immediately before the Omicron wave, allows for

characterization of immunity from previous infections. This density and quality of data is uncommon among

unvaccinated populations, especially during the Omicron variant wave when large proportions of the Canadian

population and other high-income countries had been vaccinated.

These estimates can help better understand immunity patterns and protection during the emergence of a new

variant, among unvaccinated populations, and can be useful for model parametrization.

### 3.13 Methods

### 3.14 Data source: Hutterite Cohort study

The Hutterite Cohort study enrolled a total of 1,849 participants across 21 Hutterite colonies in Alberta and

Saskatchewan, Canada, with an initial phase November 19, 2020, to June 4, 2021, and extension phases in July 11,

2021, to November 9, 2021; January 5, 2022, to July 24, 2022; February 2, 2023, to June 26, 2023. All individuals of

any age living on Hutterite colonies in Alberta and Saskatchewan that agreed to participate in the study by the start

date, November 19, 2020, were eligible, provided informed consent or assent for children was obtained. There were

no exclusion criteria.

Demographic information including age, sex, past medical history, medications, and vaccine history were

obtained at enrollment. Of 1,849 participants, 2% reported having received a COVID-19 vaccine. A self-collected

flocked nasal swab, a collection method previously validated and used extensively in the Hutterite community,

was collected at baseline from all participants. Nasal swabs were collected weekly from participants over the study

period, whether symptomatic or not. Serum was obtained for antibody testing at baseline and at the end of the study

period. Infection with SARS-CoV-2 was confirmed with real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), where

the amplification targets were the envelope gene and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene (limit of detection <

10 copies/reaction) on nasal samples collected weekly. IgG antibody titers (using recombinant SARS-CoV-2 spike

RBD) were obtained from serum samples collected at the beginning, middle and end of each study phase.

The protocol was approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board, the ethics review board at the

University of Calgary, and the ethics review board at the University of Saskatchewan. Participants gave written

39


<!-- Page 52 -->


informed consent. Participants provided consent for children, and assent was also directly sought from children

aged 7 to 15 years.

### 3.15 Data coding

We focus our analysis on the study phase from January to July 2022 which coincides with the rise in infections

with the Omicron variant in Canada. Firstly, based on weekly PCR testing against SARS-CoV-2 between January

2022 and May 2022, each week we define participants as infected and infectious (I) the first time they test positive,

and susceptible (S) otherwise. Secondly, we use serological testing in January 2022 as indicator of immunity from

prior infection.

We restrict our analysis to study participants for whom we have serology results at the beginning of the phase.

As participants are considered not to have been infected on weeks without test results, we restrict the analysis to the

study participants that test regularly, defined as 10 tests or more during the phase. Furthermore, as participants build

an immune response after getting infected with the Omicron variant, we censor them after they become infected.

We include them as part of the category with high antibody titer in a sensitivity analysis in Appendix 3.25. As these

restrictions lead to small sample sizes in some colonies, we exclusively run our analysis in colony-weeks where >50%

non-previously infected participants test. We vary this cutoff from 30% - 70% in a sensitivity analysis in Appendix

3.24.

3.15.1 Notation

We count in each colony-week the number of individuals in the following categories:

• S0 t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with antibody titers under a threshold (type 0) at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• S1 t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with antibody titers above a threshold (type 1) at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• I0 t−1: the number of newly infected individuals of type 0 at time t −1, potential infectors for time t.

• I1 t−1: the number of newly infected individuals of type 1 at time t −1, potential infectors for time t.

• I0 t : the number of newly infected individuals of type 0 at time t.

• I1 t : the number of newly infected individuals of type 1 at time t.

• SX t−1: the number of susceptible individuals with titer X at time t −1, potential infectees for time t.

• IX t : the number of newly infected individuals with titer X at time t.

To estimate the dose-response relationship between antibody titers from infection-derived immunity and

3.15.4 Parameter estimation/inference

We use MLE to estimate values of a, y, and β in the first analysis and τ, and β in the second. We conduct

the estimation in stan using the cmdstanr package (version 0.8.1.9000) in R (version 4.4.2). Standard errors and

confidence intervals around parameter estimates are obtained using stan’s Laplace algorithm. All code used in this

study is publicly available on Github.

### 3.18 Estimation of protection from infection-derived immunity

3.18.1 Immunity to susceptibility and infectiousness

infection using a binary antibody titer threshold. We find that the odds ratio for the relative susceptibility of people

### 3.19 Discussion

We use a rich and unique dataset of residents of Hutterite colonies that were followed intensely in 2022 during

the rise of Omicron in Canada to provide insight into the strength and mechanism of immune protection derived

through COVID-19 infection. The quantity of surveillance data is unmatched in a completely unvaccinated pop-

ulation, with most participants adhering extremely well to weekly PCR testing, which is done independently of

symptoms. This allows us to have probably very limited under-reporting or reporting bias. In addition, this study

had collected serology before the spread of Omicron, allowing for evaluation of immunity from prior infection.

This is not dependent on previous infection having been symptomatic or recorded, and focusing on titer values

allows to not have to make assumptions on timing of infection or waning.

We found that people with antibodies from prior infection had a 31% reduction in susceptibility (0R: 0.69

(95% CI : 0.53; 0.91)). This is consistent with the other studies that have evaluated the protection conferred by

pre-Omicron infection-derived immunity against re-infection with Omicron variant, among unvaccinated people.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 studies, Stein et al. found that among unvaccinated people, protection

from past infection against re-infection with Omicron was 45.3% (95% CI: 17.3-76.1%)80. In another meta-analysis,

Bobrovitz et al. found that previous infection protects against Omicron infection by 69.5% (52.9-75.9%) at 3 months,

which drops to 24.7% (16.4-35.5%) by 12 months (10 studies)81. In a third meta-analysis using 5 studies, Hu et al.

calculated a pooled incidence rate ratio for naturally acquired antibodies against reinfection with Omicron variant

of 0.61 (0.42-0.87)82.

Considering a dose-response relationship, we found that antibody titers are associated with a decrease in the risk

of infection, with a 40% decrease in risk for medium antibody titers (the threshold we use for the binary analysis) and

up to 66% for the highest titers. Few other studies have investigated how antibody titers from pre-Omicron infection

can serve as correlate of protection from re-infection with Omicron variant, among unvaccinated people. Perez-Saez

et al. showed that the hazard ratio for Omicron infection seems to decrease with total antibodies (IgG/A/M) against

the receptor binding domain of spike protein, without being statistically significant83. Zambrana et al. found that

titers in spike-binding assay were not associated with Omicron infection, but were protective against symptomatic

49


<!-- Page 62 -->


infection, adjusting for prior vaccination and prior infection, in a population that is 32% unvaccinated85. Hollister

et al. measured antibody binding to both receptor binding domain (RBD) and S2 subunit domain (S2) of the spike

protein. They found that among unvaccinated individuals, each three-fold increase in RBD and S2 titer value was

estimated to reduce the odds of reinfection by 23% (0.65, 0.92) and 18% (0.64, 1.04), respectively86.

We have found that the leaky model was the best fit, meaning that immune protection from prior infection is

dependent on the force of infection. This is consistent with the only other study that looked at this question. In

Connecticut correctional facilities, Lind et al. found that protection from prior infection was lower when contact

was closer, suggesting that the protection may be leaky89. This result confirms that interventions to limit the intensity

of contacts can help limit transmission, even with the emergence of a very transmissible and immune-escaping

variant like Omicron.

We did not find people with immunity from prior infections to be significantly less infectious (OR: 0.88 (95%

CI: 0.57; 1.39)). This could be due to small effect size or data limitation. This result is consistent with three other

studies that have investigated how infection-derived immunity impacts infectiousness, which have found variable

results, with small or non-significant reductions.

Among contacts in California state prisons, Tan et al. estimated that prior infection reduced an unvaccinated index

case’s risk of transmitting by 23% (95% CI: 3–39%)90. Using contact tracing data from Geneva Switzerland, Mongin

et al. estimated that previous infection in the index case reduced the secondary attack rate (SAR) during the Omicron

wave by 4.3% (95% CI: 1.3-7.3%)91. Lastly, using surveillance data from residents of Connecticut correctional facilities

during the Omicron period, Lind et al. found that the prior infection status of the index case was associated with a

non-significantly lower hazard of SARS-CoV-2 transmission following close contact at the cellblock level (HR: 0.52

(95% CI: 0.27–1.03)) and cell level (HR: 0.72 (95% CI: 0.25–2.03))89.

Our work is subject to several limitations. Firstly, while we have weekly testing data from January to July

2022, our restriction on the percentage of people needing to test for a given colony-week to be included in the

analysis results in us using only a portion of the data. Most of the colony-weeks contributing to the analysis are in

January-March, and only one colony (269) contributes data in April. The duration of follow-up is limited and we do

not consider longer-term protection. Secondly as we do not always know when participants were initially infected,

we only use antibody titer values and not timing of infection. Thirdly, as we restrict our dataset to the people that

participated in serology testing in January 2022, and then further restrict to people very frequently testing by PCR,

we only have data on a portion of each of the colony and assume that they are exchangeable with people not testing.

50


<!-- Page 63 -->


We show in Appendix section 3.22 that the adults included in our analysis do not differ by age or gender from the

rest of the adult population.

Limitations are also caused by our modeling approach, which relies on several simplifying assumptions. First,

the use of Binomials assumes that each participant comes into contact with every other colony member. This

assumption may be reasonable, especially for aerosol contact, as in Hutterite communities residents work and share

meals together, the children under 15 years old attend school together, and everyone gathers for daily church service.

Second, in the binary analysis, grouping people into two categories based on antibody titers is a drastic simplification.

However, we test a range of thresholds between the two groups and then model a more complicated and realistic

dose-response relationship. Third, both of the dose-response models assume that the log odds of infection vary

linearly with titer dilutions. We verify the validity of the assumption in a sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 3.26.

Fourth, we only consider individuals to be in the infected and infectious category for one week, on the first week

they test positive, and even if they keep testing positive the following week (8% do). This is a necessary assumption

as people can keep testing positive by PCR and no longer be infectious. We do not consider variation in duration of

infectiousness as we do not have any data that could inform this parameter.

The methods we propose here could be applied to future epidemics or variant emergence with serology and

virological testing available.

## 4

## Conclusion

In these three chapters, I have used mathematical modeling to better understand the immune response to

SARS-Cov-2, and to evaluate and compare vaccine allocation policies, with a specific attention to including equity

in models. While the picture of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has changed since some of these analyses were initially

published, or when the data for Chapter 3 was collected in Hutterite colonies, these chapters illustrate how powerful

of a tool modeling can be. The lessons for equity in modeling from Chapter 2 and the methods to estimate natural

immunity combining serological and virological data from Chapter 3 are specifically aimed to be used to help future

models for epidemics to come.

In Chapter 1 I showed that, once health-care workers and people older than 75 are vaccinated, prioritizing

allocation of COVID-19 vaccines for 65-74 year olds saves both more lives and more years of life in each racial/ethnic

group than prioritizing front-line workers, in the United States as a whole and in nearly every state. In Chapter 2, I

highlight that only few vaccine allocation models took equity into account and I provide examples of how modeling

can be used to answer equity-related questions. I also argue that future vaccine allocation models should take equity

considerations into account and highlight advice for how to do so. In Chapter 3, I estimate how infection-derived

immunity protects against Omicron infection. I find that antibody titers from antecedent infection are associated

52


<!-- Page 65 -->


with a decrease in the risk of re-infection of up to 66% for the highest antibody titer values. I also investigate the

possible mechanism of protection and find that a leaky model fits the data best, which suggests that the immune

protection from prior infection is dependent on the force of infection.
